To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CI listeners do show a deficit in voice perception, which extends beyond the previously reported poor perception of F 0 and is likely related to poor spectral resolution, and that this deficit is likely related to the poor performance of CI listeners in competing speech perception.

the just-noticeable-difference (JND) in fundamental frequency (F0), the voice cue that relates to voice pitch, was about five times larger in cochlear implant users than in normal-hearing listeners, whereas the JND in vocal-tract length, the voice cue that is related to formant frequencies, was more than four times larger.
CI listeners have poor sensitivity to F0 differences and even poorer sensitivity to VTL differences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the perception of voice pitch and vocal-tract length by cochlear implant users.
the perception of speech in noise by users of cochlear implants.
the development and testing of a novel method of improving speech intelligibility of cochlear implant listeners.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in addition to the well-known F0-related deficits, the limited access to VTL in CIs leads to a significant deficit in voice perception, with implications for a number of everyday situations, such as in a noisy restaurant or in the presence of competing speakers, and, hence for speech perception in noise.
, in CI listeners, the voice perception deficit seems to stem from poor sensitivity to VTL, while F0 perception remains intact.
CI users have limited access to voice cues in speech, and that this limitation may be responsible for a range of deficits in speech perception.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although CI listeners can perceive F0 and VLT, the JNDs are too large to be useful for speech perception.
CI users are able to use both voice cues, but the cues are perceived at a coarser level, which is likely related to their limited spectral resolution.

CI listeners have a significant deficit in voice pitch and vocal-tract length discrimination that is likely related to the limited spectral resolution of the device and that this deficit is likely to contribute to the difficulties in speech perception.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CI signal is likely to be too impoverished to allow for robust perception of the full range of voices in speech, which may be a key factor limiting speech intelligibility in noise.
CI users are not as sensitive to VTL cues as NH listeners, which may be a contributing factor in their difficulties with competing speech perception.
CI listeners have a significant difficulty in perceiving the voice characteristics of the speaker.
